parts: I want to talk a bit about conventions, I know we discussed a bit previously but I want to delve deeper.  In "pure" twistor theory / older literature, they use A, B and A', B' for two component spinor indices, but in newer literature I frequently see \alpha, \beta and \dot{\alpha}, \dot{\beta} for spinor indices.  It seems to me that this was introduced by Ed Witten when he wrote a paper combining string theory and twistor theory, and it seems the string theory community prefers the \alpha, \dot{\alpha} notation, and also seems to be more consistent with the supersymmetry literature.  I think because of the popularity of string theory this seems to be the dominant convention these days, although I do see some relatively recent papers written by people based in England that still seems to use the older notation when writing about pure twistor theory, although it seems that even they might be adopting the new conventions.  What do you think about this?

Your analysis is spot on. The shift from the older twistor notation \(A, B\) and \(A', B'\) for two-component spinor indices to the newer \(\alpha, \beta\) and \(\dot{\alpha}, \dot{\beta}\) notation seems to have gained traction primarily due to the influence of Edward Witten's work in twistor-string theory and its intersections with supersymmetry and string theory【22†source】. 

The \(\alpha, \dot{\alpha}\) notation aligns more naturally with the conventions used in supersymmetry literature, where spinor indices are explicitly separated into left-handed (\(\alpha, \beta\)) and right-handed (\(\dot{\alpha}, \dot{\beta}\)) components, which makes manipulations in supersymmetric field theories more transparent. Since string theory has had a dominant influence on theoretical physics, particularly in amplitudes and gauge theory, this notation has effectively become the standard in many communities.

You're also correct in observing that older literature from the UK, particularly from mathematicians and physicists with strong ties to traditional twistor theory, still retains the \(A, B\) and \(A', B'\) notation. However, even some of those researchers seem to be transitioning to the newer conventions, possibly due to the increasing overlap of twistor techniques with modern amplitude methods and superstring theory【23†source】.

If you're writing a paper and trying to decide which convention to use, it depends on your audience. If you're engaging with the pure twistor theory community, sticking with the older notation might be fine. But if your work connects with string theory, amplitudes, or supersymmetric field theory, using \(\alpha, \dot{\alpha}\) is probably the better choice for clarity and alignment with contemporary literature. 

Do you have a strong preference yourself, or are you still weighing the advantages of each?
